individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: The paper proposes a framework for extreme blind image restoration (EBIR) that decomposes the ELQ-to-HQ mapping into two steps: a trainable projector that maps extremely low-quality (ELQ) inputs to a less-degraded low-quality (LQ) manifold, followed by a frozen pretrained BIR model for LQ-to-HQ restoration. The training is guided by an 'Image Restoration Information Bottleneck' (IRIB) loss derived from an Information Bottleneck perspective, combining an LQ reconstruction term and an HQ prior-matching term. They also introduce Look Forward Once (LFO), an inference-time prompt refinement strategy, and demonstrate plug-and-play enhancement of existing BIR models (OSEDiff, SeeSR, S3Diff) on synthetic extreme degradations.
Strengths: Novel decomposition of EBIR into ELQ->LQ->HQ, leveraging frozen pretrained models and training only a lightweight projector, which stabilizes training and reduces the search space.
The IRIB loss is a theoretically-inspired objective combining blur-aware LQ reconstruction and diffusion-based HQ prior matching; ablations show a trade-off between fidelity and perceptual quality.
Plug-and-play integration with multiple existing BIR models (OSEDiff, SeeSR, S3Diff) yields consistent improvements in perceptual/realism metrics without finetuning the backbone.
The LFO prompt refinement provides further gains in perceptual metrics and exposes an intermediate space for auxiliary refinement.
Extensive experiments with multiple metrics and ablation of the blur weight.
Weaknesses: The information-theoretic interpretation is not rigorously justified: the 'compression' of LQ to HQ is counterintuitive since HQ has more entropy; the IRIB loss reduces to a beta-VAE objective with an additional fidelity term, and the novelty of the theoretical perspective is overstated.
The experimental evaluation is limited to synthetic degradations from the Real-ESRGAN pipeline; no real-world extreme degradation benchmarks are considered.
The main comparison is only against a fine-tuned OSEDiff baseline; no other state-of-the-art EBIR or two-stage methods are compared, so the relative improvement is unclear.
The proposed LFO yields very small quantitative gains (e.g., MUSIQ +0.3, FID -0.2) and may not justify the extra inference cost.
The approach requires the frozen backbone to be a single-step model (e.g., OSEDiff) for gradient flow during training, limiting applicability to multi-step diffusion restoration models.
The paper does not provide detailed implementation of the IRIB losses (e.g., how the KL term is computed with deterministic networks, how the score-matching loss is applied to the output of g).
Questions: How does the IRIB objective relate to the standard information bottleneck when the bottleneck variable Z has higher cardinality/entropy than X?
How is the KL term in IRIB computed in practice when q_phi(z|x) is deterministic?
What is the effect of prompt dropout in training? Is the model sensitive to the dropout rate?
Why are PSNR/SSIM slightly lower than the fine-tuned baseline? Is the perceptual improvement consistent across all images or only for certain degradation levels?
How does the method perform on real-world extremely degraded images beyond synthetic pipelines?
What is the computational overhead of LFO during inference, and is it worth the marginal metric gains?
How are the ELQ degradation ranges defined compared to the LQ setting? Could the method be applied without retraining to even more severe degradations?
Limitations: The pretrained IR model g must be a single-step model for training the projector; multi-step diffusion models are not supported.
The prompt extraction module Y is not optimized for ELQ inputs and may produce suboptimal prompts.
The method is evaluated only on synthetic degradations from the Real-ESRGAN pipeline; real-world extreme degradation performance is not assessed.
The intermediate LQ manifold is tied to the specific degradation pipeline used in training (Real-ESRGAN), limiting generalization to unseen degradation types.
The gains from LFO are marginal and the additional inference cost may not be justified in all applications.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: The paper addresses Extreme Blind Image Restoration (EBIR), where inputs suffer from severe compounded degradations. The authors propose a decomposition framework that first trains a projection module f_theta to map extremely low-quality (ELQ) images to an intermediate low-quality (LQ) manifold, then applies a frozen off-the-shelf BIR model g for LQ-to-HQ restoration. They ground this approach in an Information Bottleneck perspective, deriving an Image Restoration Information Bottleneck (IRIB) loss that combines an LQ reconstruction term with an HQ prior-matching term, plus a sample-wise HQ fidelity loss. They also introduce Look Forward Once (LFO), an inference-time prompt refinement strategy that uses intermediate LQ samples to iteratively improve text conditioning. Experiments on synthetic extreme degradations (based on the Real-ESRGAN pipeline) with OSEDiff, SeeSR, and S3Diff show perceptual quality improvements (e.g., FID, MUSIQ, CLIPIQA) at a slight cost in PSNR/SSIM, and demonstrate plug-and-play enhancement of existing BIR models without finetuning.
Strengths: The decomposition of EBIR into ELQ->LQ->HQ is a sensible strategy to reduce ill-posedness and enables the reuse of frozen pretrained restoration models in a plug-and-play manner.
The blur-aware LQ reconstruction and HQ fidelity terms with a tunable lambda_blur provide a practical mechanism to trade off fidelity and perceptual quality.
The paper demonstrates consistent perceptual improvements across multiple backbone models (OSEDiff, SeeSR, S3Diff) in the tested synthetic extreme-degradation settings.
The proposed LFO prompt refinement is simple and provides a small but consistent perceptual gain with minimal overhead.
Weaknesses: The Information Bottleneck framing is not rigorously derived: the IRIB loss is essentially a beta-VAE-style cycle-consistency objective, and the actual training loss includes an ad-hoc HQ-fidelity term not justified by the IB theory.

The notation in Section 4 is confusing and incomplete; the roles of q_phi and q_psi, and how they relate to the deterministic f_theta and g, are never clearly specified, making the method difficult to reproduce.
The experimental evaluation is limited to synthetic degradations following the Real-ESRGAN pipeline; no real-world extreme low-quality images are tested, which is the core motivation of EBIR.
The method requires the frozen restored model g to be a single-step generator; multi-step diffusion models cannot be directly used, a significant practical constraint.

The reported PSNR/SSIM are generally lower than the fine-tuned OSEDiff baseline, and the perceptual improvements come from a systematic fidelity-perceptual trade-off rather than an overall improvement across all metrics.

The gains from LFO are very small (e.g., CLIPIQA changes of 0.002-0.003), and the paper does not provide an analysis of the computational overhead or the conditions under which LFO is most beneficial.
Questions: What exactly are q_phi and q_psi in Eq. (14)? How are they implemented, and are they separate networks or part of f_theta and g? The paper never describes a stochastic encoder/decoder despite the probabilistic notation.

How are the paired (x^(E), x) generated during training? Is x the standard LQ image corresponding to the same HQ target, and is x^(E) the extreme LQ image from the same HQ? The data pipeline needs clarification.
What is the empirical contribution of the HQ-prior term versus the HQ-fid term? Only lambda_blur is ablated; the individual loss terms are not studied, making it unclear which component is essential.

When applying the trained projector to SeeSR or S3Diff, how does the projector trained with OSEDiff as the frozen g remain compatible? Does the intermediate LQ manifold truly depend only on the degradation, as claimed?
What is the additional computational cost of LFO, and how does the prompt extraction module Y perform on extremely degraded inputs? Is there a risk of error accumulation with iterative refinement?
Limitations: The framework is restricted to single-step pretrained restoration models, as multi-step diffusion models would require backpropagation through many steps.
The reliance on a shared degradation pipeline (Real-ESRGAN) limits generalization to other degradation types, and no real-world extreme degradation evaluation is provided.
The prompt extraction module Y is likely inaccurate on extremely degraded inputs, which may limit the effectiveness of LFO; the paper notes this as a limitation.

The theoretical contribution is overstated; the IB analogy does not yield a novel algorithm beyond a weighted combination of existing losses (cycle-consistency, score distillation, and supervised fidelity).

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: The paper addresses Extreme Blind Image Restoration (EBIR), where images suffer from severe compounded degradations. It proposes to decompose the ELQ-to-HQ restoration into two steps: first train a projector mapping ELQ to an intermediate LQ manifold, then apply a frozen pretrained blind restoration model to map LQ to HQ. The authors derive an Image Restoration Information Bottleneck (IRIB) loss combining LQ reconstruction and HQ prior matching, and introduce Look Forward Once (LFO) for iterative prompt refinement. The framework supports plug-and-play enhancement of existing BIR models. Experiments on synthetic extreme degradations show improvements in perceptual metrics and realism, with minor trade-offs in pixel fidelity.
Strengths: The decomposition ELQ->LQ->HQ with a frozen BIR model effectively reduces the ill-posedness of extreme blind restoration and is practical.
The IRIB loss combines LQ reconstruction and HQ prior matching in a way that yields good perceptual results, even if the theoretical grounding is not fully rigorous.
The LFO prompt refinement leverages the intermediate LQ representation for better conditioning and iterative refinement improves perceptual metrics.

The plug-and-play integration with existing BIR models (SeeSR, S3Diff) shows that the projector generalizes across models sharing the same degradation pipeline, extending their applicability to extreme degradations.
The paper provides thorough quantitative evaluation with multiple metrics and ablations on the trade-off between fidelity and perceptual quality.
Weaknesses: The theoretical connection to Information Bottleneck is not rigorously established; the IRIB loss is essentially a beta-VAE-like objective with a deterministic encoder, and the KL term is replaced by diffusion score matching without a clear derivation.
The method assumes a known degradation model (Real-ESRGAN) and requires the frozen BIR model to be trained on the same degradation distribution, limiting generalization to unseen degradations.
The experimental validation uses only synthetic degradations; no real-world ELQ images are tested.
The quantitative improvements of LFO are marginal (e.g., MUSIQ gains <0.5), and PSNR/SSIM are slightly lower than the fine-tuned baseline, without statistical significance tests.
The paper does not report computational cost or inference overhead, which is important for practical deployment.
The writing contains inconsistencies (e.g., notation in Eq 13, typos) and the derivations in Section 4.2 are unclear in connecting the theoretical terms to the practical losses.
Questions: How is the HQ prior matching loss in Eq (17) derived from the KL divergence in Eq (14)? What is the exact relationship between the diffusion score-matching objective and the KL term?
Since the projector and the frozen model both use OSEDiff with LoRA adapters, can you detail the architecture differences and the number of trainable parameters?

The plug-and-play experiments with SeeSR and S3Diff use the same trained projector. How does the projector ensure that its output lies in the LQ manifold expected by these different models? Is the shared degradation model sufficient?
Can the method handle completely blind scenarios where the degradation is not from the Real-ESRGAN pipeline? How does it perform on real-world low-quality images?
What is the inference time overhead of LFO? How many iterations are needed for optimal results?
Limitations: The pretrained IR model must be a single-step model for training the projector due to gradient flow; this limits application to multi-step diffusion models.
The prompt extraction module is not robust for ELQ inputs, which may constrain performance.
The method is specific to the Real-ESRGAN degradation pipeline and may not generalize to other degradations without retraining.

The projector is trained with a fixed g; the sensitivity to the choice of g is not analyzed, and the plug-and-play generalization across different g models is only shown for models sharing the same degradation.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: The paper addresses Extreme Blind Image Restoration (EBIR) by decomposing the ELQ-to-HQ mapping into two stages: a trainable projector f_theta maps extreme low-quality (ELQ) images to an intermediate low-quality (LQ) manifold, and a frozen, off-the-shelf BIR model maps that LQ image to high quality. The method is framed as an Information Bottleneck problem, leading to the proposed IRIB loss that combines an LQ reconstruction term and an HQ prior-matching term. The paper also introduces Look Forward Once (LFO), an inference-time prompt refinement strategy, and demonstrates plug-and-play enhancement of existing BIR models without fine-tuning them. Experiments on DIV2K/DIV8K show perceptual quality improvements over direct ELQ-to-HQ fine-tuning and off-the-shelf baselines.
Strengths: The decomposition into an intermediate LQ manifold is a practical and intuitive way to reduce the ill-posedness of EBIR, and the plug-and-play integration with frozen BIR models is useful and broadly applicable.
LFO is a lightweight inference-time refinement that exploits the intermediate LQ representation and shows consistent improvement in perceptual metrics.
The blur-aware losses and the lambda_blur ablation demonstrate an explicit and controllable trade-off between pixel fidelity and perceptual realism.
Quantitative results on DIV2K and DIV8K show that the proposed method improves LPIPS, DISTS, FID, MUSIQ, and CLIPIQA over direct fine-tuning, with only a small PSNR/SSIM penalty.
Weaknesses: The Information Bottleneck derivation is not rigorous: the 'representation' Z is an HQ image rather than a compressed variable, and the roles of q_phi, q_psi, X, Y, and Z are inconsistent; the connection to beta-VAE is superficial and not formally justified.
The paper contains clear technical errors, e.g., Eq. (21) defines \hat{x}_{LQ}^{(1)} = g(f_theta(x_ELQ; c^{(1)})) even though g maps LQ to HQ, contradicting the text that says it is the LQ image.

The training objective is under-specified: the precise definitions of q_phi, the student noise predictor in L_HQ-prior, and the paired HQ target z in L_HQ-fid are unclear; how gradients flow through the frozen g while training only f_theta is not detailed.

Experimental comparison is narrow: the main table compares only to OSEDiff and its fine-tuned variant, with no comparison to other recent BIR/EBIR methods or to an end-to-end model with matched compute; no statistical significance or confidence intervals are reported.
Ablations are limited to lambda_blur; the individual contributions of the LQ reconstruction term, HQ prior term, and LFO are not systematically ablated.

Reproducibility is hindered by missing details: exact extreme degradation parameter ranges, architecture of f_theta, prompt dropout specifics, and the relationship between RAM-based training prompts and DAPE-based test prompts are not provided.
Questions: In Eq. (21), should \hat{x}_{LQ}^{(1)} be f_theta(x_ELQ; c^{(1)}) rather than g(f_theta(...))? If not, how is the LQ image obtained from the HQ output of g?

What exactly are q_phi and q_psi in Eq. (14)? Are they fixed components of the frozen BIR model g, part of the degradation simulator D, or newly introduced networks? How are their parameters set if only theta is optimized?

How is the HQ prior matching loss L_HQ-prior implemented in practice? Which network serves as the student noise predictor \hat{\epsilon} and which as the fixed HQ prior's noise predictor \hat{\epsilon}_{HQ}? Is an additional network trained?

The paper claims an Information Bottleneck perspective, but the derivation seems to map LQ to HQ to LQ, where the 'representation' is an HQ image rather than a compressed variable. Can you clarify the formal mapping to the IB Lagrangian and why the beta-VAE analogy holds?

What are the exact ranges of the extreme degradation settings (resizing factors, blur kernel sizes, noise levels, JPEG quality) relative to the default Real-ESRGAN configuration? Without these, the experiments are not reproducible.

In LFO, the prompt extracted from the LQ image is used to condition the ELQ-to-LQ mapping. Since the input ELQ image is unchanged, why would a prompt derived from the LQ image be more suitable than one derived from the ELQ image?

For plug-and-play with SeeSR and S3Diff, f_theta is trained with OSEDiff as the frozen g. How does the transfer to different g models work given that their trained LQ distributions may differ slightly?
Could you provide an ablation that removes the LQ reconstruction term or HQ prior term to verify their individual necessity, and an ablation of LFO that isolates its effect from the projector?
What is the computational overhead of the projector and LFO in terms of parameters and inference time compared with the baseline OSEDiff?
Limitations: The method requires a single-step frozen BIR model for training because gradients must flow through the model multiple times for multi-step diffusion models (acknowledged by the authors).
The prompt extraction module is not optimized for ELQ inputs and may produce suboptimal prompts (acknowledged by the authors).
The framework is only validated on synthetic degradations following the Real-ESRGAN pipeline; generalization to real-world extreme degradations is not demonstrated.

The plug-and-play claim assumes that different pretrained BIR models share the same input LQ distribution; this is only approximately true and not explicitly verified for models trained with different degradation pipelines.

The paper does not discuss potential negative societal impacts, such as the use of restored images to misrepresent evidence from low-quality surveillance footage or the risk of hallucinating details that are presented as authentic.

review.Summary: The paper addresses Extreme Blind Image Restoration (EBIR), where inputs suffer from severe, compounded degradations beyond the training scope of existing BIR models. The authors propose a decomposition of the intractable ELQ-to-HQ mapping into two stages: a learnable projector maps ELQ images to an intermediate, less-degraded LQ manifold, and a frozen pretrained BIR model then maps this LQ image to HQ. The method is grounded in an Information Bottleneck perspective, leading to the Image Restoration Information Bottleneck (IRIB) loss that combines an LQ reconstruction term and an HQ prior-matching term. The framework also introduces Look Forward Once (LFO), an inference-time prompt refinement strategy, and supports plug-and-play enhancement of existing BIR models without finetuning the backbone. Experiments on synthetic extreme degradations show that the proposed method improves perceptual quality over baselines while preserving structural fidelity, and that it can be applied to different pretrained models.
Strengths: The decomposition of extreme restoration into ELQ->LQ->HQ stages is practical and helps mitigate the ill-posedness of direct ELQ-to-HQ mapping.
The Information Bottleneck perspective offers a unifying theoretical lens and leads to a loss that couples LQ reconstruction with HQ prior matching.
The plug-and-play capability is demonstrated with multiple existing BIR models (OSEDiff, SeeSR, S3Diff), showing broad applicability without retraining the backbone.
Look Forward Once is a novel inference-time refinement technique that leverages the intermediate LQ representation for better prompt conditioning.
Weaknesses: The theoretical connection to Information Bottleneck is not rigorously established. The IRIB loss reduces to a beta-VAE-style objective, and the claimed 'degrade-back' simulation is essentially a cycle-consistency term, while the prior-matching term (Eq. 17) is a diffusion noise-prediction loss rather than a KL divergence, making the mapping to the IB bound unclear.

Experimental validation is narrow. Only synthetic Real-ESRGAN degradations are used, there is no comparison with other dedicated extreme-restoration methods, and the gains are modest: the proposed method often has lower PSNR/SSIM than a fine-tuned baseline, and perceptual improvements (FID, MUSIQ, CLIPIQA) are small.

LFO refinement yields negligible quantitative differences across iterations (e.g., MUSIQ changes by <0.1), and no statistical significance tests are provided to support the claim that recursive refinement helps.

The presentation is sometimes confusing: equations have broken formatting, notation is inconsistent (e.g., ${\mathcal{D}}$ vs $D$), and many figures/tables are redacted or referenced but not visible, hindering reproducibility assessment.

The claim of 'without finetuning' is misleading: while the backbone is frozen, the projector $f_{\theta}$ is trained, so the full pipeline requires training. The plug-and-play advantage is only for the backbone, not the entire system.
Questions: How is Eq. 17 derived from the KL divergence term in the IRIB objective? Specifically, how does the noise-prediction loss correspond to KL$(q_{\phi}(z|x) \parallel r(z))$?
In Eq. 14, what is the exact parametrization of $q_{\phi}$? Is $z$ a deterministic function of $f_{\theta}(x^{(E)})$? If so, why use an expectation over $q_{\phi}$?
Why is blur-MSE used in both the LQ reconstruction and HQ fidelity terms? Could this over-regularize and cause the projector to ignore high-frequency details that might be recoverable?
Are the LFO improvements statistically significant? Were paired tests or multiple runs conducted to assess variance?

In the plug-and-play experiments, is the projector $f_{\theta}$ shared across different backbones (OSEDiff, SeeSR, S3Diff)? If so, does the intermediate LQ manifold align across these models, and how is this alignment ensured?

What is the effect of the degradation ${\mathcal{D}}$ used in the LQ reconstruction term? If it is the same as the extreme degradation, how does the projector avoid simply copying the input? If it is the original LQ degradation, what guarantees the intermediate output lies in the manifold expected by the backbone?
Limitations: The method currently requires a single-step pretrained restoration model since gradients must flow through the backbone; multi-step diffusion models are not directly supported.
The prompt extraction module may produce unreliable prompts on severely degraded images, limiting the effectiveness of LFO.
All experiments use synthetic degradations from the Real-ESRGAN pipeline; generalization to real-world extreme degradations remains untested.
The projector is trained on a specific degradation distribution; distribution shifts at test time could degrade performance.

The framework can hallucinate details in extreme restoration, which could be misused for generating misleading images or fabricating evidence, though this is a general concern for generative restoration methods.

review.Summary: The paper addresses Extreme Blind Image Restoration (EBIR) by decomposing the ELQ-to-HQ mapping into two stages: a trainable projector f_theta maps extremely low-quality (ELQ) images to an intermediate low-quality (LQ) manifold, and a frozen pretrained BIR model maps that LQ image to high quality. The method is motivated by an Information Bottleneck perspective, leading to the proposed Image Restoration Information Bottleneck (IRIB) loss that combines LQ reconstruction and HQ prior-matching terms. The paper also introduces Look Forward Once (LFO), an inference-time prompt refinement strategy. Experiments on synthetic extreme degradations show perceptual quality improvements for several frozen BIR models (OSEDiff, SeeSR, S3Diff) at a slight cost in PSNR/SSIM.
Strengths: The decomposition ELQ -> LQ -> HQ with a frozen pretrained BIR model is a practically useful way to reduce the ill-posedness of extreme blind restoration and enables plug-and-play enhancement without fine-tuning the backbone.
The blur-aware LQ reconstruction and HQ prior-matching losses allow an explicit, tunable trade-off between pixel fidelity and perceptual realism.
Consistent perceptual improvements (e.g., FID, MUSIQ, CLIPIQA) are demonstrated across multiple backbones (OSEDiff, SeeSR, S3Diff) in the tested synthetic degradation settings.
The proposed LFO prompt refinement is a lightweight inference-time technique that provides consistent, albeit small, perceptual gains.
The overall framework is original in combining an intermediate LQ manifold with frozen BIR models, and the plug-and-play capability is a useful contribution for practical restoration systems.
Weaknesses: The Information Bottleneck (IB) framing is not rigorously established: the IRIB loss reduces to a beta-VAE-style cycle-consistency objective plus an ad-hoc HQ-fidelity term and a diffusion score-matching prior; the formal connection to an IB bound is unclear and the notation for q_phi and q_psi is never concretely specified.
The experimental evaluation is limited to synthetic degradations from the Real-ESRGAN pipeline; no real-world extreme degradation benchmarks are considered, though this is a core motivation for EBIR.

The comparison is narrowly scoped: the main quantitative comparison is against a fine-tuned OSEDiff baseline, with no other dedicated EBIR or two-stage methods, leaving the relative improvements unclear.
LFO yields very small quantitative gains (e.g., MUSIQ changes <0.5, CLIPIQA changes ~0.002-0.003), and no statistical significance tests are reported.
The method requires the frozen restoration model to be a single-step generator (e.g., OSEDiff) for gradient flow during training, preventing direct use of multi-step diffusion restoration models.

Several implementation details are under-specified, including the exact degradation ranges for ELQ, the architecture of f_theta, how the prompt dropout is applied, and how the LQ reconstruction loss avoids trivial copying of the input.
Questions: How exactly are q_phi and q_psi in Eq. (14) instantiated? Are they separate stochastic encoders/decoders or deterministic functions of f_theta and g? The probabilistic notation is never backed by an actual stochastic model.
In Eq. (21), should \hat{x}_{LQ}^{(1)} be f_theta(x_ELQ; c^{(1)}) rather than g(f_theta(...))? As written, it appears to output an HQ image, contradicting the LQ label.
How is the score-matching/HQ prior-matching term in Eq. (17) derived from the KL divergence in Eq. (14)? What is the exact relationship between the diffusion noise-prediction loss and the KL term?

How does the projector trained with OSEDiff as the frozen g transfer to SeeSR and S3Diff? Is the intermediate LQ manifold aligned across these models solely because they share the Real-ESRGAN degradation pipeline?
What are the exact extreme degradation parameter ranges (resize factors, blur kernels, noise levels, JPEG quality) used in training and evaluation? Without these, experiments are not reproducible.
Are the LFO improvements statistically significant? Were multiple runs or paired tests performed to quantify variability?
What is the computational overhead of the projector and LFO in terms of parameters and inference time?
Can the method generalize to real-world extreme degradations or to degradation types not represented by the Real-ESRGAN pipeline?
Limitations: The pretrained restoration model must be a single-step generator for training, ruling out multi-step diffusion models unless approximation strategies are used.
The prompt extraction module is not optimized for ELQ inputs and may produce suboptimal prompts, limiting the effectiveness of LFO.
All experiments use synthetic degradations generated by the Real-ESRGAN pipeline; generalization to real-world degradation distributions is untested.
The intermediate LQ manifold is tied to the specific degradation distribution used in training, so distribution shifts at test time could degrade performance.
The reported PSNR/SSIM are often lower than the fine-tuned baseline, indicating a systematic fidelity-perceptual trade-off rather than universal improvement.
The marginal gains from LFO may not justify the additional inference cost in all practical settings.
Potential misuse of hallucinated details in extreme restoration for misrepresenting evidence is a general concern for generative restoration methods, though the paper does not discuss it.
